new.title: Walk the white terraces of De Kiefhoek
new.desc: Architect J.J.P. Oud built De Kiefhoek between 1928 and 1930 as municipal housing: around 290 small homes in long, repeating rows. It is a textbook example of the Dutch Nieuwe Bouwen and was reconstructed between 1990 and 1995.
new.tip: One house, at Hendrik Idoplein 2, is kept as a museum home; check ahead when it can be visited. The streets themselves are always open.

new.title: Eat lunch from a guest cook at Verhalenhuis Belvédère
new.desc: Verhalenhuis Belvédère on Katendrecht is a house of stories, with exhibitions on its upper floors and a small stage. In its Volkskeuken a different guest cook makes lunch every day from Tuesday to Sunday.
new.tip: Lunch is served while supplies last, so come early. Closed on Mondays.

new.title: Take the kids to Plaswijckpark
new.desc: Plaswijckpark began in 1923 as a tea garden and walking park on the Bergse Achterplas, started by a Rotterdam restaurateur. It has grown into about 15 hectares of playgrounds, a small animal park and boat trips, popular with families with young children.
new.tip: It is open all year, with shorter hours in winter and an indoor playground for wet days. Buy tickets online.

new.title: Spread a blanket in the Vroesenpark
new.desc: The Vroesenpark is the park of Blijdorp, in the triangle between the Kanaalweg, Vroesenlaan and Stadhoudersweg. Work started in 1929 to a plan by city architect Witteveen, and after a new design by landscape architect Bijhouwer it reopened in 1958.
new.tip: The Vroesenpaviljoen stands in the south-west corner. The zoo is next door if you want to make a day of it.

new.title: Have brunch by the water on the Zaagmolenkade
new.desc: De Brunch Club sits on the Zaagmolenkade in the Oude Noorden, with a terrace by the water. It serves breakfast, brunch and lunch only: egg dishes, smoothie bowls, a sandwich with oyster mushroom croquettes and good coffee.
new.tip: It is walk-in only and the kitchen closes at 15:30. It shuts on some midweek days, so check first.

new.title: Sit on the lakeside terrace of De Tuin
new.desc: Café-restaurant De Tuin occupies a stately house from 1867 on the edge of the Kralingse Plas, between the two windmills. Its big waterside terrace fills up as soon as the sun comes out.
new.tip: It is open every day for lunch and dinner. Come by bike or on foot through the Kralingse Bos; parking at the lake is paid.

new.title: Find Rotterdam's first public park, the Oude Plantage
new.desc: Laid out by the city in 1769, the Oude Plantage was the first public park in Rotterdam. It is a small, little-used strip of green between the Maasboulevard and the river, with views over the Nieuwe Maas and the skyline.
new.tip: Few people come here, so you may have a bench to yourself. It is open all year.

new.title: Watch Sparta play at Het Kasteel
new.desc: Sparta, founded in 1888, plays in Spangen at a ground opened in 1916. The stadium is called Het Kasteel after the small two-towered building behind one stand, the only part of the original design that survives; the club won six national titles, the last in 1959.
new.tip: With about 11,000 seats it is a far more intimate afternoon than De Kuip. Walk around to see the castle building before kick-off.

new.title: Pick a slice of carrot cake at Koekela
new.desc: Koekela has been baking American-style cakes since 2003, all made in-house, and its Rotterdam shop is on the Nieuwe Binnenweg. The carrot cake with cream cheese frosting is the classic, with lemon meringue pie and the cheesecakes close behind.
new.tip: It is open seven days a week. Sharing two slices between two is the way to taste more.

new.title: See the last city gate of Delft, the Oostpoort
new.desc: Delft once had eight city gates; the Oostpoort is the only one left, after the others were pulled down around 1840. It dates from about 1400 and was raised in 1519.
new.tip: The inside is not open to the public, so this one is about the view from the outside, with the gate reflected in the water.

new.title: Lunch at the Stads-Koffyhuis on the Oude Delft
new.desc: The Stads-Koffyhuis is a long-running lunch café on the Oude Delft canal in Delft. It is known for its long list of sandwiches and pancakes, and names its local suppliers, from the farm to the flour mill, on its website.
new.tip: It is open seven days a week but is a daytime place, so come for breakfast, lunch or high tea. On fine days the terrace fills quickly.

new.title: Glide through Delft on a canal boat
new.desc: From April to the end of October canal boats leave the Koornmarkt every hour for a tour of about 50 minutes through the old centre. A live guide tells the stories of Delft Blue, Vermeer, Van Leeuwenhoek and the House of Orange.
new.tip: Tickets are sold at the kiosk at Koornmarkt 113. Departures start at 11:00, and the boats have a glass roof that closes on showery days.

new.title: Eat from the kitchen garden at Villa Augustus
new.desc: Villa Augustus is a hotel and restaurant in Dordrecht's water tower of 1882, the second oldest in the country, and its former pumping station. Since 2007 the kitchen has cooked with the seasons from the vegetable garden laid out around it, beside the Wantij.
new.tip: Walk through the garden before or after your meal; it is part of the experience. Reserve a table ahead.

new.title: Visit the Hof van Nederland in Dordrecht
new.desc: In 1572 Dordrecht hosted the First Free Assembly of the States, an early step towards an independent Netherlands. Museum Hof van Nederland, in the Hof where it took place, is about Dutch freedoms then and now.
new.tip: Check opening days on the museum's website before you go. It is in the old centre, so it fits easily into a walk around the harbours.

new.title: Explore Fort Buitensluis on the Hollandsch Diep
new.desc: In the south of the Hoeksche Waard, an earthwork was built in 1793 beside the harbour lock of Numansdorp to watch shipping on the Hollandsch Diep. It was strengthened in the 1860s and again in 1915 with concrete, and was used for military and police training until 2014.
new.tip: From May to September the fort is open on weekend afternoons, free of charge, with guided tours on the second weekend of the month.

new.title: Swim off the gentle beach at Rockanje
new.desc: The beach at Rockanje on Voorne faces mostly south, so it catches the sun, and sandbars offshore break up the waves into calm water over a gently sloping seabed. That makes it a favourite with families; there are five beach pavilions and the dunes of Voornes Duin right behind.
new.tip: The main entrances with big car parks are the 1e Slag and 2e Slag. For more space, head for the quieter stretch to the south.
